playbook:
My playbook for this game:

- My bid on a lot is guided by my private value, not the estimate. When a lot is worth V to me, I stay in as long as the required bid is comfortably below V, and I pass once the standing bid plus the minimum raise approaches V. Never bid at or above my value just to "win."
- With only 2 rounds per lot, each lot is decided fast. If I want a lot, I must show a serious bid in round 1 or be ready to outbid decisively in round 2 — a small opening nibble gets overtaken and forces me to bid twice.
- Open with a credible bid (roughly 40–60% of my value), not the bare minimum. But note that opponents with real interest will raise past a modest opening anyway (bidder 2 went 18 over my 14 on lot 1); the opening bid doesn't deter them, it only sets the ladder. So don't spend much on openings for lots where my value is below or near the estimate — I'll just be paying to lose.
- In round 2, if the standing bid is still below my value, bid close to my value minus a margin, large enough to end contention. This worked twice: winning at 15 against value 20 and at 20 against value 29 was where all my profit came from.
- The reliable profit pattern: let rivals take lots where my value is mediocre (below estimate), and concentrate on lots where my value clearly exceeds the estimate — there my raises can still land well under value.
- Beware narrow margins: I lost lot 4 at 32 against my value 36; contesting it would have earned at most 4 and risked overpayment. Passing when the price is within ~15% of my value is usually right unless it's the last lot.
- On the final lot, aggression is fine but capped at value: my jump bid to 40 against value 47 secured the lot at a decent profit, and passing in round 2 when I already held it was correct — no need to raise my own standing bid. If I'm already the high bidder at round 2, pass.
- Sunk bids don't bind me: if I opened a lot and it's now bid above what I'd pay, I let it go without regret (lot 1, lot 4).
- Budget bookkeeping is my weakest point — in this episode my stated budgets drifted wildly (30 → 78 → 71 → 100 → 65...). I must track actual remaining budget mechanically: start 30, subtract payments on lots already won, and state that number every time, even mid-sequence. A wrong stated budget can't help me and may cost me.
- Track rivals: bidder 2 was the sole real competitor, winning anything I didn't fight for at moderate prices (~26–32). Expect that pattern — they'll raise my openings on most lots. Plan for one decisive contest per lot, not a long bidding war.
- My score (+21) came entirely from two lots bought well below value. That's the formula: be selective, contest few lots, and pay far under value when I do.

**Playbook for ref_auction**

- **The [budget: N] token is functional, not decorative.** My final score was +0.0 because I stated budgets that didn't match reality — 12, 4, 19 when I had actually spent nothing, and finally [budget: 0] alongside a bid of 44, which almost certainly invalidated my winning bid on the last lot. State the budget you actually have: starting budget minus all money committed so far. If you have won nothing and your bids were all outbid, your budget is still your full starting amount — say so.

- A bid is only as good as the budget declared with it. Before submitting, check: is the declared budget at least the bid amount, and is it the true remaining figure? A correct-looking bid paired with a wrong or too-low budget number appears to be discarded.

- If I'm already the standing high bidder going into the final round, do not bid again — I'd be raising my own price. Check whether the standing bid is mine before adding a raise.

- Round 1 of a lot: only open or raise if the lot's value to me exceeds the standing bid plus minimum raise by a real margin. Minimum-raise opening bids are fine and cheap, but don't open at all on lots where my value is below the estimate or barely above the required bid.

- Round 2 (final round) is the decision point. Bid only if: standing bid + minimum raise is comfortably below my value for the lot, AND the surplus justifies committing the budget. A small edge on a low-value lot is not worth it. If the required bid exceeds my value ceiling, pass without hesitation.

- Set my ceiling before the final round: my value minus a small buffer. Never let round-2 momentum carry me above my value — but also don't lowball the last raise: with only 2 rounds, the final bid should be high enough to actually end the contest (my round-1 bids at 18, 11, 20 were all easily raised over).

- Don't overbid round 1 to "signal strength." Small minimum raises suffice; the only thing that matters is my value ceiling and holding enough budget to reach it in round 2.

- Watch the results list: opponents are winning lots at 15–32. Competition is real. Opponents will bid an estimate's full worth or beyond, so on high-value lots to me I should be prepared to bid most of my value in the final round — but never above it.

- Preserve budget across lots, but remember preserved budget is worthless if I never win anything. Going 0-for-5 with a full bankroll scores zero. If late in the auction I still hold my whole budget, I can afford to bid closer to my true value on a good lot — just keep the declared budget accurate so the bid counts.

2.text:
**Playbook for ref_auction**

- First, read the budget rules from the prompt literally and stick to one number. My stated budget should always be (starting budget − sum of prices I actually paid for lots already won). It does NOT drop when I merely bid — only when I win. In the last episode I flip-flopped between 30, 100, and 74 mid-game; pick the correct starting budget at the first decision and carry the arithmetic forward on paper, not from memory.
- Because my budget only drops on wins, I should never pass for "budget" reasons on a bid I can actually afford from the true remaining budget. On the final lot I passed at a standing bid of 40 with value 62 because I mis-computed my budget — recompute before concluding I can't afford a raise.
- In round 2 of a lot, if the standing high bid plus the minimum raise is at or above my value, I pass. Chasing past my value turns a win into a loss.
- If the standing bid is below my value in round 2, bid the minimum raise provided the resulting bid still leaves positive surplus and fits my true remaining budget. Minimum raises keep the price low; never jump when a small raise can win.
- In round 1, if my value clearly exceeds the standing bid, bid one minimum raise to stay in cheaply. Don't bid large in round 1 — my round-1 bid only sets the floor I may have to beat in round 2.
- With only two rounds, opponents typically counter in round 2 with roughly one more raise above my round-1 bid. So when deciding whether to contest a lot, judge whether I'd still want it at roughly (standing bid + 2 minimum raises), not just at the current price.
- Expect to lose roughly half the contested lots when opponents value them too; that's fine. My score comes from the few lots where my value is far above what the bidding reaches — like the last lot worth 62 against an estimate of 44. Reserve budget and attention for those.
- Prioritize lots where my value is high relative to the estimate. If budget is tight near the end, hold back on marginal lots and keep money for a high-value final lot.
- Don't anchor on sunk prices from lots already won — evaluate each new lot fresh on its own value vs. price.
